lesson.title: Writing the Line in the Language of the Problem
lesson.summary: The regression equation dresses up y-hat equals b0 plus b1x in the real units and variable names of the study, so the slope and intercept carry meaning, not just symbols.
lesson.body:
A regression line only becomes useful once it is written down as an equation that can be shared, checked, and applied to new values by someone who never saw the original scatterplot. The standard form is y-hat equals b0 plus b1 times x, where the small hat placed over the y is a deliberate piece of notation: it signals a predicted value coming out of the model, not an actually observed value from the data.

Plugging in the numbers found earlier, b0 equal to 39 and b1 equal to 10, gives y-hat equals 39 plus 10x. That version is mathematically complete but communicates almost nothing about the actual study to an outside reader. A usable regression equation replaces the generic symbols with the real variable names and units: predicted exam score equals 39 plus 10 times hours studied. Written this way, anyone reading it, not just the person who built the model, understands immediately what is being predicted from what, and with which units.

Units matter more here than they did for correlation. Recall that r stayed at 0.99 no matter what units were used for hours studied, because rescaling x and y rescales their standard deviations by the same factor and the z-scores underneath r are unaffected. The regression slope does not enjoy that same protection: it changes value whenever the units of x or y change, because a slope is expressed as a rate, points per hour in this case, not as a unitless ratio like r.

To see this directly, suppose hours studied had instead been recorded in minutes, so every x-value is multiplied by 60. The slope becomes 10 divided by 60, or about 0.167 points per minute, since the exact same overall rise in score now has to be spread across 60 times as many x-units on the new scale. The line still describes exactly the same underlying relationship and would generate identical predictions for the same student regardless of which units were used, but the numeric value of the slope itself depends on the units chosen, so stating those units alongside b1 is never optional.

The intercept is subject to the same requirement, even though it is easy to forget. Reporting b0 as simply 39 leaves out the fact that this 39 is measured in points, the units of the response variable, not in hours at all. A complete statement reads: when hours studied equals 0, predicted exam score equals 39 points. Both coefficients in a regression equation inherit units from the original variables in this way, the slope combines the units of y and x into a rate, while the intercept simply carries the units of y alone, which is one more way the regression equation differs fundamentally from the unitless correlation coefficient computed several chapters earlier.

With a complete, correctly labeled equation in hand, the next two chapters unpack precisely what the slope and the intercept mean in the context of this study, before a later chapter puts the equation to work making actual numerical predictions for new students.
